article.body:
Think of an automated thermostat in a smart building that must follow strict energy-saving rules while deciding on its own when to cool a room during an unexpected heatwave. Our computer workers examined how systems divide their internal resources between planning strategies and executing actions to handle such dual pressures. Paper-supported readings suggest that systems work best when they partition, which means separate, these heavy reasoning tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. [1]

The teams recorded how these systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings indicate that failure attribution, which means tracking down specific errors across multi-step agent trajectories, helps isolate decisive error steps and understand reasoning limits. [2]

Researchers looked into hybrid architectures for autonomous problem formulation, noting that autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [3]

When examining high-stakes scenarios, analysts found that strict directive adherence becomes a failure of intelligence when it ignores safety-critical constraints in high-stakes decision scenarios. [4]

Investigations into preference formation show that cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions and information in real-time. [5]

Studies on human-computer interaction also highlight that AI-driven training recommendation reliance correlates with reduced self-regulation and increased decision hesitation in athletes, pointing to a serial causal chain where outsourcing body signals leads to reduced autonomy. [6]

Work on foundational assumptions indicates that general preference oracle formulations provide a rigorous basis for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [7]

Additional memory studies suggest that episodic memory recall provides temporal credit assignment structures that stabilize preference formation in sequential decision tasks. [8]

Exploring curiosity, teams noted that curiosity arousal mechanisms dynamically guide exploratory behavior and shape emergent agent preferences. [9]

To handle multiple conflicting goals, systems utilize Pareto-Conditioned Proximal Policy Optimization, which means an optimization method that enables agents to learn portfolios of non-dominated policies, facilitating dynamic objective prioritization. [10]

Furthermore, value system learning from demonstrations in multi-agent reinforcement learning can leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [11]

Finally, computational creativity frameworks depend upon a structured decomposition of problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

article.body:
Think of an automated thermostat in a smart building that must follow strict energy-saving rules while deciding on its own when to cool a room during an unexpected heatwave. Our computer workers examined how systems divide their internal resources between planning strategies and executing actions to handle such dual pressures. Paper-supported readings suggest that systems work best when they partition, which means separate, these heavy reasoning tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. [1]

The teams recorded how these systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings indicate that failure attribution, which means tracking down specific errors across multi-step agent trajectories, helps isolate decisive error steps and understand reasoning limits. [2]

Researchers looked into hybrid architectures for autonomous problem formulation, noting that autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [3]

When examining high-stakes scenarios, analysts found that strict directive adherence becomes a failure of intelligence when it ignores safety-critical constraints in high-stakes decision scenarios. [4]

Investigations into preference formation show that cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions and information in real-time. [5]

Studies on human-computer interaction also highlight that AI-driven training recommendation reliance correlates with reduced self-regulation and increased decision hesitation in athletes, pointing to a serial causal chain where outsourcing body signals leads to reduced autonomy. [6]

Work on foundational assumptions indicates that general preference oracle formulations provide a rigorous basis for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [7]

Additional memory studies suggest that episodic memory recall provides temporal credit assignment structures that stabilize preference formation in sequential decision tasks. [8]

Exploring curiosity, teams noted that curiosity arousal mechanisms dynamically guide exploratory behavior and shape emergent agent preferences. [9]

To handle multiple conflicting goals, systems utilize Pareto-Conditioned Proximal Policy Optimization, which means an optimization method that enables agents to learn portfolios of non-dominated policies, facilitating dynamic objective prioritization. [10]

Furthermore, value system learning from demonstrations in multi-agent reinforcement learning can leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [11]

Finally, computational creativity frameworks depend upon a structured decomposition of problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance planning, following rules, and adapting to new information. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely adapt when unexpected changes occur.

Abstract
We investigated the potential utility of large language models (LLMs) in supporting patient safety efforts. Specifically, we evaluated the reasoning capabilities of LLMs in performing root cause analysis (RCA) of radiation oncology incidents using narrative reports from the Radiation Oncology Incident Learning System (RO-ILS). We prompted four state-of-the-art LLMs, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o, o3, and Grok 3, with the “Background and Incident Overview” sections from 19 publicly available RO-ILS cases. Each model was instructed to perform RCA and generate root causes, lessons learned, and suggested actions using a standardized prompt based on AAPM RCA guidelines. Model outputs were evaluated using a combination of objective semantic similarity metrics (cosine similarity via Sentence Transformer), semi-subjective assessments (precision, recall, F1-score, expert-adjudicated PPV (Positive Predictive Value), hallucination rate and performance criteria including relevance, comprehensiveness, quality of justification and quality of solution), and subjective ratings (reasoning quality and overall performance) by five board-certified medical physicists. LLMs demonstrated satisfactory performance across evaluation metrics. All models exhibited some degree of hallucination, ranging from 11% to 61%. All the evaluated LLMs demonstrated comparable baseline capabilities in objective causal extraction, and Gemini 2.5 Pro exhibited the highest overall performance score among 4 models. Statistically significant differences were observed among models in expert-adjudicated PPV, hallucination rate, and subjective ratings (
p
< 0.05). LLMs delivered promising results as assistive tools for RCA in radiation oncology, with the ability to generate relevant and accurate analyses aligned with expert expectations. LLMs may support incident analysis and contribute to quality improvement efforts to advance patient safety in clinical radiation oncology practice.

Abstract
We investigated the potential utility of large language models (LLMs) in supporting patient safety efforts. Specifically, we evaluated the reasoning capabilities of LLMs in performing root cause analysis (RCA) of radiation oncology incidents using narrative reports from the Radiation Oncology Incident Learning System (RO-ILS). We prompted four state-of-the-art LLMs, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o, o3, and Grok 3, with the “Background and Incident Overview” sections from 19 publicly available RO-ILS cases. Each model was instructed to perform RCA and generate root causes, lessons learned, and suggested actions using a standardized prompt based on AAPM RCA guidelines. Model outputs were evaluated using a combination of objective semantic similarity metrics (cosine similarity via Sentence Transformer), semi-subjective assessments (precision, recall, F1-score, expert-adjudicated PPV (Positive Predictive Value), hallucination rate and performance criteria including relevance, comprehensiveness, quality of justification and quality of solution), and subjective ratings (reasoning quality and overall performance) by five board-certified medical physicists. LLMs demonstrated satisfactory performance across evaluation metrics. All models exhibited some degree of hallucination, ranging from 11% to 61%. All the evaluated LLMs demonstrated comparable baseline capabilities in objective causal extraction, and Gemini 2.5 Pro exhibited the highest overall performance score among 4 models. Statistically significant differences were observed among models in expert-adjudicated PPV, hallucination rate, and subjective ratings (
p
< 0.05). LLMs delivered promising results as assistive tools for RCA in radiation oncology, with the ability to generate relevant and accurate analyses aligned with expert expectations. LLMs may support incident analysis and contribute to quality improvement efforts to advance patient safety in clinical radiation oncology practice.

Discussion
Our study demonstrates the promising, albeit still developing, reasoning capabilities of leading LLMs when applied to the complex task of RCA for radiation oncology incidents. The findings indicate that LLM models can generate RCAs that exhibit considerable alignment with expert-derived analyses. Additionally, the evaluated LLMs achieved favorable expert-rated performance overall, with some differences across models in hallucination rates and subjective quality ratings. This suggests an emerging potential for LLMs to assist in the initial stages of incident analysis, potentially streamlining the process for human experts.

article.body:
Think of an automated thermostat in a smart building that must follow strict energy-saving rules while deciding on its own when to cool a room during an unexpected heatwave. Our computer workers examined how systems divide their internal resources between planning strategies and executing actions to handle such dual pressures. Paper-supported readings suggest that systems work best when they partition, which means separate, these heavy reasoning tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. [1]

The teams recorded how these systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings indicate that failure attribution, which means tracking down specific errors across multi-step agent trajectories, helps isolate decisive error steps and understand reasoning limits. [2]

Researchers looked into hybrid architectures for autonomous problem formulation, noting that autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [3]

When examining high-stakes scenarios, analysts found that strict directive adherence becomes a failure of intelligence when it ignores safety-critical constraints in high-stakes decision scenarios. [4]

Investigations into preference formation show that cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions and information in real-time. [5]

Studies on human-computer interaction also highlight that AI-driven training recommendation reliance correlates with reduced self-regulation and increased decision hesitation in athletes, pointing to a serial causal chain where outsourcing body signals leads to reduced autonomy. [6]

Work on foundational assumptions indicates that general preference oracle formulations provide a rigorous basis for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [7]

Additional memory studies suggest that episodic memory recall provides temporal credit assignment structures that stabilize preference formation in sequential decision tasks. [8]

Exploring curiosity, teams noted that curiosity arousal mechanisms dynamically guide exploratory behavior and shape emergent agent preferences. [9]

To handle multiple conflicting goals, systems utilize Pareto-Conditioned Proximal Policy Optimization, which means an optimization method that enables agents to learn portfolios of non-dominated policies, facilitating dynamic objective prioritization. [10]

Furthermore, value system learning from demonstrations in multi-agent reinforcement learning can leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [11]

Finally, computational creativity frameworks depend upon a structured decomposition of problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance planning, following rules, and adapting to new information. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely adapt when unexpected changes occur.

article.body:
Think of an automated thermostat in a smart building that must follow strict energy-saving rules while deciding on its own when to cool a room during an unexpected heatwave. Our computer workers examined how systems divide their internal resources between planning strategies and executing actions to handle such dual pressures. Paper-supported readings suggest that systems work best when they partition, which means separate, these heavy reasoning tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. [1]

The teams recorded how these systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings indicate that failure attribution, which means tracking down specific errors across multi-step agent trajectories, helps isolate decisive error steps and understand reasoning limits. [2]

Researchers looked into hybrid architectures for autonomous problem formulation, noting that autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [3]

When examining high-stakes scenarios, analysts found that strict directive adherence becomes a failure of intelligence when it ignores safety-critical constraints in high-stakes decision scenarios. [4]

Investigations into preference formation show that cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions and information in real-time. [5]

Studies on human-computer interaction also highlight that AI-driven training recommendation reliance correlates with reduced self-regulation and increased decision hesitation in athletes, pointing to a serial causal chain where outsourcing body signals leads to reduced autonomy. [6]

Work on foundational assumptions indicates that general preference oracle formulations provide a rigorous basis for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [7]

Additional memory studies suggest that episodic memory recall provides temporal credit assignment structures that stabilize preference formation in sequential decision tasks. [8]

Exploring curiosity, teams noted that curiosity arousal mechanisms dynamically guide exploratory behavior and shape emergent agent preferences. [9]

To handle multiple conflicting goals, systems utilize Pareto-Conditioned Proximal Policy Optimization, which means an optimization method that enables agents to learn portfolios of non-dominated policies, facilitating dynamic objective prioritization. [10]

Furthermore, value system learning from demonstrations in multi-agent reinforcement learning can leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [11]

Finally, computational creativity frameworks depend upon a structured decomposition of problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance planning, following rules, and adapting to new information. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely adapt when unexpected changes occur.
article.lede: Our computer workers are investigating how independent systems balance strict instructions with the need to adapt when situations change unexpectedly.
article.lens: We look at how computational systems process complex rules and unexpected changes by reviewing current research papers and technical frameworks.
article.title: Tracing How Intelligent Systems Handle Unexpected Choices and Rules

Motivation

Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses.

Results

We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. Motivation

Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses.

Results

We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. MR-MAS leverages the reasoning and coordination capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and integrates external tools to unify data acquisition, causal effect estimation, results interpretation, and manuscript preparation into a single workflow, thereby reducing manual effort. MR-MAS further incorporates a structured Mendelian Randomization Knowledge Base (MRKB) to support MR method implementation and targeted repair of MR analysis code. Across diverse test scenarios, MR-MAS demonstrated stable workflow execution, reproduced several literature-supported causal signals, and maintained consistent causal estimates across repeated runs and different model backends. Additional evaluations showed robust trait retrieval and improved code-repair performance with MRKB guidance. These results suggest that MR-MAS may provide practical support for scalable, standardized, and reproducible MR analyses in biomedical research.
